:::

## What you should be able to do tonight

- State the three defining properties of Brownian motion and say which of them a scaled random walk satisfies in the limit.
- Say why the paths are continuous everywhere and differentiable nowhere, in terms of the scaling between time and displacement.

## Tasks <span class='task-total'>60 min</span>

::: {.task-list}
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [30 min]{.task-min} Read the first chapter of Etheridge's Oxford stochastic calculus notes, on the construction of Brownian motion from a random walk. It is written for people who know probability, which saves you the two weeks a finance-first treatment would cost.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [20 min]{.task-min} Build the limit yourself: simulate a symmetric random walk with n steps over a fixed time interval, scaling the step size as the square root of the time increment, for n of 100, 10,000 and 1,000,000. Plot all three paths on the same time axis and note that the picture stops changing qualitatively.
:::
::: {.task}
<input type="checkbox" class="task-check"> [10 min]{.task-min} Show the non-differentiability numerically: for one path, compute the ratio of the increment to the time step at increasingly fine resolution, and watch it diverge. The square-root scaling is exactly what makes that ratio blow up.
:::
:::
